headline: Race Point on the last of the ebb: bass to 34 pounds on live mackerel
subhead: The rip did the work this week — mackerel schools thick enough to snag, bass stacked underneath, and a Barnstable bluefish pattern building fast.
body_markdown:
Tuesday morning I had a father-son charter out of Provincetown, and I told them before we even cleared the breakwater — we're not running far, we're drifting Race Point on the last two hours of the ebb, and we're going to let the rip do the talking. That's how I've fished that water for thirty years and I'm not changing now. We snagged a few mackerel off the surface with a Diamond Jig rig maybe half a mile off the Point, hooked two live ones on 5/0 circle hooks under a fish-finder rig, and dropped them right into the seam where the color changes from that deep green to the churned-up white water. Twenty minutes in, the kid's rod buried and we came up with a 34-pound bass, fat and chrome, right off the structure at Peaked Hill Bars. That's the pattern right now and it's a good one — not easy, but good.

The rips off Race Point and Peaked Hill Bars have been holding bass all week, but you have to fish the stages right. Dead low and dead high, forget it — the water goes flat and the fish scatter off the structure. It's that last push of the ebb and the first hour of the flood where the current stacks bait against the sand bars and the bass move up to feed. Live mackerel is still the best bait out there, hands down, but I've had guys do well drifting umbrella rigs with tube teasers through the same water when the macks weren't cooperating. Depth's been 15 to 25 feet right on the bars, deeper — 30 to 40 — just off the edges where the drop-off meets the rip.

What I like about this time of year up here is that Cape Cod Bay doesn't shut down the way the water does south of the Cape. The Gulf of Maine keeps feeding cooler water in around the Race and along the backside, and that keeps the stripers willing to feed through the middle of the day, not just at first light. I've had good bites at noon on some of these drifts when guys down the coast are telling me their bass have gone nocturnal. Doesn't mean it's a free-for-all — you still want moving water and you still want to be on structure, not just anywhere in the Bay. But it's forgiving compared to what I hear from the Sound side.

Bluefish have been building in the harbors and creek mouths around Barnstable and Sandy Neck, and this is exactly the pattern I figured we'd see start to show — the peanut bunker have spread into those back-bay flats and the cocktail blues are tracking them in tight. Nothing giant, two to four pounds mostly, but steady, and fun on light spinning gear. Small metal — half-ounce to one-ounce Kastmasters, or a Deadly Dick if the current's got any push to it — worked on the drop of the tide through the channel edges off Sandy Neck has been putting fish in the boat pretty reliably in the last hour of daylight. If you're throwing topwater at dusk off the beach there, don't be surprised if you get bit on almost every cast for a stretch and then it just stops — that's the bait moving through, not the fish leaving.

Fluke fishing has been steady but not spectacular in the channels around Barnstable Harbor and out toward Sandy Neck flats. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on quarter-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the sandy bottom in 12 to 18 feet, been picking at keepers in the two-to-four-pound range. Nothing to write home about size-wise, but if you're patient and cover water on the drift you'll put a few in the cooler.

Cod's a different story right now. Billingsgate and the deeper structure out toward the Stellwagen edge haven't been holding much — this is typically a fall pattern for us up here, once the water starts to turn over and cool, and August just isn't the month. I wouldn't waste a trip on it yet. Give it another six weeks.

We're coming off a full moon this week, and that's put some real push into the tides — bigger swings, harder current on the rips, which has actually sharpened up the bite windows at Race Point rather than blowing them out. As that current eases over the next several days, I'd expect the bass to spread a little wider off the bars and the bite to soften up some, so if you've got a window this weekend, I'd take it. Best case, the mackerel schools hold tight off the Point and the bass stay stacked underneath them through the week. If the macks push off — and sometimes they do, chasing their own bait — I'd shift over to trolling tube-and-worm through the same rip structure rather than chasing bait around trying to snag it. Either way, fish the moving water, fish the structure, and don't be in a hurry. That's the whole game out here.
